title: How can technology assist visual disorders? Focus and clarity faults, glasses, contact lenses, laser surgery and lens replacement
subtitle: Half the world may be short-sighted by 2050, and many older people's lenses turn cloudy. How can technology assist visual disorders?
subject: Biology
lessonIntent: tracing light through the cornea (most of the bending, fixed) and the lens (fine focus) to the retina, whose light-sensitive cells send signals along the optic nerve; explaining accommodation (the ciliary muscle contracts, the lens rounds and bends light more for near objects); explaining myopia and hyperopia as a mismatch between the eye's bending power and its length, with which distances blur and why; astigmatism as an unevenly curved cornea; presbyopia as a stiffened lens that cannot accommodate; a cataract as a clouded lens that scatters light, a clarity fault that glasses cannot clear; how concave and convex lenses in glasses or contact lenses move the focus, and the infection risk of contacts; how LASIK flattens the cornea for myopia, and its limits (irreversible, stable prescription and corneal thickness needed, dry eye and glare, no effect on presbyopia); how lens replacement restores clarity, and its limits (no accommodation, so reading glasses; small infection risk; needs a working retina); matching each technology to the fault and the person; applying this to a changing myopic prescription and to a cataract.

voiceover.text: By 2050, about half the people in the world may be short-sighted, if current trends continue. In most of those eyes, the fault is tiny: light comes to a sharp point a millimetre or so in front of where it needs to land. Other eyes focus perfectly well, but the light can't get through clearly. So how can technology assist visual disorders?

Light enters the eye through the cornea, its clear, curved front, which does most of the bending. The lens behind it bends the light a little more and fine-tunes the focus. The light should meet at a sharp point on the retina, a layer of light-sensitive cells at the back, which send signals along the optic nerve to the brain. For a near object, a ring of muscle around the lens contracts, the fibres holding the lens go slack, and the lens rounds up to bend light more. That's accommodation.

Clear vision needs the eye's bending power to match its length. In myopia, or short-sightedness, the eyeball is usually too long, or the cornea too steeply curved. Light from a distant object comes to a point in front of the retina, then spreads out again, so distant things look blurred. Light from a near object is already spreading as it arrives, so it focuses further back, on the retina, and near things look clear. To remember it: with myopia, you see what's near "my" eyes.

In hyperopia, or long-sightedness, it's the other way round. The eyeball is usually too short, or the cornea too flat, so light would come to a point behind the retina. Near objects blur most. In astigmatism, the cornea is curved more in one direction than another, so there's no single sharp point. And from about the mid-forties, the lens stiffens and can't round up for close work. That's presbyopia, and it's why many people need reading glasses.

Some faults aren't about focus at all. A cataract is a lens that has turned cloudy. Proteins in the lens clump together, so instead of passing straight through, light is scattered. Vision becomes dim and blurred, colours fade, and headlights cause glare. Ageing is the main cause, and sunlight, smoking and diabetes can raise the risk. So the eye might focus perfectly, but the light can't get through clearly, and glasses can't clear a cloudy lens.

For a focus fault, change how light is bent before it reaches the retina. Glasses do it from outside the eye. For myopia, a concave lens, thinner in the middle, spreads the light a little, moving the focus back onto the retina. For hyperopia and for reading, a convex lens, thicker in the middle, bends light inward, moving the focus forward. For astigmatism, a toric lens bends light differently in different directions. Contact lenses do the same job on the cornea, moving with the eye for a wider clear view. But worn overnight or cleaned poorly, they can let an infection into the cornea.

Laser surgery changes the eye itself. In LASIK, a thin flap is cut in the surface of the cornea and folded back. A laser then removes a precise amount of tissue underneath. For myopia, it takes more from the centre, flattening the cornea so it bends light less, and the focus moves back onto the retina. The flap is laid back and heals without stitches. But the change is permanent. It needs a stable prescription and a thick enough cornea, it can cause dry eyes and glare at night, and it doesn't stop presbyopia, because it doesn't change the lens.

For a cataract, the fix is to replace the cloudy lens. Through a tiny cut, ultrasound breaks up the old lens, and it's removed. A folded artificial lens, made of clear plastic, is slipped in and opens into place. Light passes through clearly again, and the new lens can also correct short- or long-sightedness. But it can't change shape, so most people still need reading glasses. There's also a small risk of infection. And it only helps if the retina still works.

So, like hearing devices, these are matched, not ranked. Glasses are cheap, safe and easy to change, so they suit almost anyone, including growing children. Contact lenses suit active people who'll keep them clean. Laser surgery suits adults with a stable prescription who want to be free of lenses. Lens replacement is the only one that helps a cloudy lens. Glasses and corneal surgery leave a long eyeball long. Cataract surgery removes the clouded lens.

Two exam questions. First. A nineteen-year-old can read their phone clearly, but lecture slides look blurred from the back of the room. Their prescription has become stronger each year for three years. Identify the disorder and explain its cause. Then explain why glasses or contact lenses suit them better than laser surgery, for now. Pause here to answer.

It's myopia. The eye's too long or too powerful, so light from the distant slides comes to a point in front of the retina, while light from the nearby phone lands on it. Their prescription is still changing, so a laser correction made now could drift, and it can't be undone. Glasses or contacts can simply be changed each year. The classic mistake is choosing laser surgery because it's permanent.

Second. A seventy-four-year-old has gradually dim, cloudy vision in one eye, and glare from headlights at night. New glasses haven't helped. An eye examination finds a cloudy lens and a healthy retina. Evaluate lens replacement surgery for this person. Pause here to answer.

This is a cataract, a clarity fault, which is why new glasses didn't help. Surgery removes the cloudy lens, and an artificial lens lets light through to the healthy retina, so clear vision can return. But reading glasses are usually still needed, and there's a small risk of infection. On balance, it's a strong choice here. The classic mistake is thinking laser surgery on the cornea would fix it.

So for any vision question, ask where the light goes wrong. If the focus misses the retina, move the focus with glasses, contact lenses or laser surgery. If the lens is cloudy, replace it. Next: what can replace lost kidney function?
